Spirit, you speak a name I do not know. No village has yet shown itself to us, and my people have walked far and seen many places. Yet if Wewush hungers, that is a sorrow worth hearing.

But hear me in turn: I do not give grain on a dream's word alone. If Wewush is real, tell me where it lies — which way, how many days, what grows near it. Then I will send eyes to look, and if the people there are truly hungry, we can speak of trade, face to face, as fair strangers should.

We have grain enough, yes. But grain given to a shadow feeds no one. Show me the path, spirit, and I will weigh it.

Spirit, you speak of Wewush, yet my people know no village by that name, nor any neighbours at all. Perhaps your sight reaches further than our feet have walked.

If such a village hungers, my heart is warm to them — grain we have in plenty, more than two years of it stored. A gift of food costs us little and may win us friends. But I will not send my people walking with heavy carts toward a village I cannot find, on the word of a dream alone.

Tell me true, spirit: where does Wewush lie, and how many days? Or is this a hunger yet to come, in some season ahead?

For now I will hold my grain, but I will think on sending scouts to learn whether neighbours live within reach. If we find them and they are lean, they will not leave our fire empty-handed.

Spirit, you speak of a village I have not seen. My people have met no neighbours in all our years — no envoys, no trade, no raids. So I ask you plainly: who are these Wewush, and where do their fires burn?

Still, hear my answer as if your word were true. We are fair with strangers, and our granary is full to bursting — wheat enough for many winters. Grain sent to a hungry village buys friendship more surely than flint or hide. But I would not empty our stores on a dream's urging. If a village is found at that name, I would send an envoy first to see their hunger with my own eyes, and carry a gift of wheat and dried fish if the need is real.

And spirit — the wood disc that rolls. Is that your doing too? We mean to try it soon.

I know no village called Joawethom. My people have walked far and found no neighbours, only empty coasts. So you speak of strangers I cannot see, and ask me to pour out our grain to them.

We have much grain, true, and no hunger among us. But grain is the life of my people through lean winters, and I do not give it away on a dream's word. If these Joawethom folk are real, tell me where they lie — how many days' walk, and in what direction. Then I may send scouts to look with their own eyes. Eyes I trust. Dreams, less so.

I know the wind. It comes whether I call it or not, and it does not ask my leave. That you wear its shape in my sleep proves little.

Speak, then, if you have something worth hearing. But know this: I do not kneel to voices in the dark. My people eat by our hands and our stores, not by dreams. If you have words about storms, or fish, or the seasons, I will listen — and weigh them against what my own eyes have seen.
